title: Stop Talking About Critical Thinking. Watch These Students Debate About Data Centers
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard, a competitive-debate coach, argues that the September-October 2026 Public Forum debate topic -- whether the federal government should enact a moratorium on hyperscale AI data-center construction -- is producing more rigorous critical thinking among middle and high school debaters than most adult public commentary manages, and uses the topic as an extended case study in what genuine critical thinking looks like in practice. He contrasts the public discourse's 'stochastic parroting' (repeating slogans like 'AI will save us' or 'we have to beat China' without examining what would make them true or relevant) against the debate round's structural demand that every claim survive a determined opponent's scrutiny and evidentiary challenge. The bulk of the piece maps the topic's actual argumentative terrain in detail -- water scarcity and contamination, electricity pricing, grid reliability, farmland loss, AI misalignment, and corporate concentration on the Pro side; economic growth, cybersecurity, medical research, and geopolitical competition with China on the Con side -- and walks through concrete argument-and-response exchanges, such as the 'golf courses use more water than data centers' comparison and how each side complicates it further. The essay's underlying claim is that critical thinking is not a general disposition to be lectured about but a skill built through structured practice defending and attacking specific, well-researched positions on a genuinely consequential question.
points: The essay's central provocation is that competitive debate students, working through 600+ pages of research on a single resolution, are demonstrably out-thinking much of the adult public discourse on AI, which mostly consists of unexamined slogans ('AI will save us,' 'we have to beat China').

Its working definition of critical thinking is operational, not aspirational: it happens when a consequential question, real research access, and an opponent obligated to challenge every claim are all present simultaneously -- not when students are simply told to 'think critically.'

The water-scarcity exchange (golf courses use more water than data centers) is used as a worked example of how a surface-level comparison gets complicated by both sides -- Con uses it to challenge singling out computing, Pro accepts the comparison while noting an industry needn't be the largest user to worsen a local shortage.

The topic's breadth -- spanning water policy, grid reliability, AI safety, corporate concentration, and US-China competition under one resolution -- is presented as forcing debaters to connect claims across domains rather than treating each argument in isolation, which is precisely the connective reasoning missing from public AI discourse.
quotes: We are only five tournaments into the season, and hundreds of middle school and high school students are already debating the details of data centers with a level of seriousness that makes much of the public conversation look ridiculous.
Saying "data centers use water" gets you to the beginning of the conversation. Where does the water come from? Is the facility in a drought-prone area? What cooling system does it use?

Meanwhile, much of the public debate consists of stochastic parroting: "AI will save us." "AI is destroying the planet." "We have to beat China." Familiar claims circulate with little examination of what would make them true, false, or relevant to a particular decision.
If we want students to think critically, this is what it looks like. Give them a consequential question, access to research, and opponents who will make them defend what they say.

The file explicitly includes the response that golf courses use more water in aggregate than data centers. Con uses this comparison to challenge the decision to single out computing. Pro can accept the comparison while pointing out that an industry need not be the largest user to worsen a shortage.

A credible Pro case identifies preventable harms and shows why a pause changes them. A credible Con case identifies benefits that depend on continued construction and shows why targeted protections or technical improvements can preserve them.
